title: Linear combination of Schrödingerization for quantum linear systems with optimal matrix-query complexity
authors: Yin Yang, Yue Yu, Long Zhang
abstract: Quantum linear systems algorithms (QLSAs) aim to solve linear systems $A\bb{x}=\bb{b}$ exponentially faster than classical methods under certain conditions. In this work, we develop quantum algorithms for solving linear algebraic equations from an ODE-based perspective. Inspired by the linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation (LCHS) representation in the Fourier approach \cite{Childs2017QLSA}, we express the solution $\bb{x}$ as a linear combination of solutions to a system of linear convection equations, which become Schrödinger-type equations with unitary evolutions in the Fourier domain. We refer to this representation as LC-Schrödingerization. Based on this result, we construct an LCHS-based quantum algorithm with two LCHS instances: one for time-marching and one for numerical integration. The key construction uses the derivative of a Gaussian-smoothed hat function and recovers the solution over a fixed auxiliary interval. This permits a truncation time independent of the target accuracy and avoids the loss in success probability from selecting a single grid point. Periodization and explicit Fourier coefficients provide the corresponding projection error bounds. Under the stated oracle assumptions and given a constant-factor estimate of the solution norm, direct simulation of the select operators and block preconditioning achieve the optimal matrix-query complexity $\mathcal{O}(κ_A\log\frac1\varepsilon)$ without using variable-time amplitude amplification (VTAA). The same upper bound holds for queries to the right-hand-side preparation oracle.
summary: This paper presents a quantum algorithm to solve linear systems $Ax=b$ by reformulating the problem using LC-Schrödingerization. The method constructs a quantum circuit based on two LCHS simulations, achieving the theoretically optimal matrix-query complexity. This advancement is significant as it provides a resource-efficient quantum tool for solving problems central to quantum simulation and computational physics.
main_problem: Developing quantum algorithms to solve linear systems of equations, $Ax=b$, with an exponential speedup over classical methods.
main_result: The authors developed an LCHS-based quantum algorithm that achieves the optimal matrix-query complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\kappa_A \log(1/\epsilon))$ without relying on Variable-Time Amplitude Amplification.
method: The solution is represented via LC-Schrödingerization, transforming the problem into a system solvable by combining two instances of the Linear Combination of Hamiltonian Simulation (LCHS) method.
model_or_system: The problem is framed from an ODE-based perspective, where the solution $x$ is the steady-state solution to $ut = -Au + b$. For indefinite $A$, the solution uses LC-Schrödingerization, which involves unitary evolutions in the Fourier domain.
key_observables: Matrix-query complexity, relative joint-vector error ($E_I$), success probability ($P_I$), and truncation error.
important_parameters: Condition number ($\kappa_A$), target precision ($\epsilon$), and the smoothing parameter ($\sigma$).
main_assumptions: Assumes oracle access for the matrix $A$ and the right-hand-side preparation oracle, and requires a constant-factor estimate of the solution norm.
figures_summary: Figures compare the performance of Gaussian versus smoothed hat kernels, showing the smoothed hat kernel achieves significantly lower relative joint-vector error and higher success probabilities for interval recovery.
paper_structure: The paper develops the LC-Schrödingerization framework, constructs the LCHS-based quantum algorithm using two LCHS instances (time-marching and numerical integration), and proves the optimal query complexity by employing block preconditioning techniques.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, theoretically optimal quantum algorithm for a fundamental problem in scientific computing (solving linear systems), directly applicable to simulating quantum dynamics or solving large-scale quantum chemistry problems.
